claim: The resurgent component of the voltage-gated sodium current (INaR) is a depolarizing conductance revealed on membrane hyperpolarizations following brief depolarizing voltage steps.
source: The resurgent component of the voltage-gated sodium current (INaR) is a depolarizing conductance, revealed on membrane hyperpolarizations following brief depolarizing voltage steps, which has been shown to contribute to regulating the firing properties of numerous neuronal cell types throughout the central and peripheral nervous systems.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a defining characteristic of INaR.

claim: INaR has been shown to contribute to regulating the firing properties of numerous neuronal cell types throughout the central and peripheral nervous systems.
source: The resurgent component of the voltage-gated sodium current (INaR) is a depolarizing conductance, revealed on membrane hyperpolarizations following brief depolarizing voltage steps, which has been shown to contribute to regulating the firing properties of numerous neuronal cell types throughout the central and peripheral nervous systems.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature establishing the functional role of INaR.

claim: INaR is mediated by the same voltage-gated sodium (Nav) channels that underlie the transient and persistent Nav current components.
source: Although mediated by the same voltage-gated sodium (Nav) channels that underlie the transient and persistent Nav current components, the gating mechanisms that contribute to the generation of INaR remain unclear.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract.

claim: The gating mechanisms that contribute to the generation of INaR remain unclear.
source: Although mediated by the same voltage-gated sodium (Nav) channels that underlie the transient and persistent Nav current components, the gating mechanisms that contribute to the generation of INaR remain unclear.
evidence: This establishes the knowledge gap that motivates the study.

claim: The voltage and duration of the initial membrane depolarization affect the amplitudes and kinetics of INaR.
source: Here, we characterized Nav currents in mouse cerebellar Purkinje neurons, and used tailored voltage-clamp protocols to define how the voltage and the duration of the initial membrane depolarization affect the amplitudes and kinetics of INaR.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2.

claim: A novel Markov kinetic state model with parallel (fast and slow) inactivation pathways reproduces the properties of the resurgent, transient, and persistent Nav currents recorded in mouse cerebellar Purkinje neurons.
source: Using the acquired voltage-clamp data, we developed a novel Markov kinetic state model with parallel (fast and slow) inactivation pathways and, we show that this model reproduces the properties of the resurgent, as well as the transient and persistent, Nav currents recorded in (mouse) cerebellar Purkinje neurons.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by the modeling results shown in Figure 3.

claim: Resurgent Na+ influx occurs as a result of fast inactivating Nav channels transitioning into an open/conducting state on membrane hyperpolarization.
source: Based on the acquired experimental data and the simulations, we propose that resurgent Na+ influx occurs as a result of fast inactivating Nav channels transitioning into an open/conducting state on membrane hyperpolarization, and that the decay of INaR reflects the slow accumulation of recovered/opened Nav channels into a second, alternative and more slowly populated, inactivated state.
evidence: This is the proposed mechanism based on experimental data and modeling simulations.

claim: The decay of INaR reflects the slow accumulation of recovered/opened Nav channels into a second, alternative and more slowly populated, inactivated state.
source: Based on the acquired experimental data and the simulations, we propose that resurgent Na+ influx occurs as a result of fast inactivating Nav channels transitioning into an open/conducting state on membrane hyperpolarization, and that the decay of INaR reflects the slow accumulation of recovered/opened Nav channels into a second, alternative and more slowly populated, inactivated state.
evidence: This is part of the proposed mechanism supported by experimental and modeling data.

claim: Extrinsic factors that affect the kinetics of fast or slow Nav channel inactivation can modulate the amplitude of INaR.
source: Additional simulations reveal that extrinsic factors that affect the kinetics of fast or slow Nav channel inactivation and/or impact the relative distribution of Nav channels in the fast- and slow-inactivated states, such as the accessory Navβ4 channel subunit, can modulate the amplitude of INaR.
evidence: This is supported by simulations shown in Figure 9.

claim: The accessory Navβ4 channel subunit can modulate the amplitude of INaR.
source: Additional simulations reveal that extrinsic factors that affect the kinetics of fast or slow Nav channel inactivation and/or impact the relative distribution of Nav channels in the fast- and slow-inactivated states, such as the accessory Navβ4 channel subunit, can modulate the amplitude of INaR.
evidence: This is supported by simulations and previous experimental data (Ransdell et al., 2017).

claim: Voltage-gated sodium (Nav) channels open rapidly on membrane depolarization and underlie the generation of action potentials in many excitable cells.
source: Voltage-gated sodium (Nav) channels open rapidly on membrane depolarization and underlie the generation of action potentials in many excitable cells, including skeletal and cardiac muscle, as well as central and peripheral neurons.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about Nav channels.

claim: The pore-forming (α) subunits of Nav channels, Nav1.1 to Nav1.9, belong to the 'S4' superfamily of voltage-gated ion channel genes.
source: The pore-forming (α) subunits of Nav channels, Nav1.1 to Nav1.9, belong to the 'S4' superfamily of voltage-gated ion channel genes (Catterall, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Catterall, 2010.

claim: Each Nav α subunit comprises four homologous domains (DI–DIV) with six transmembrane spanning segments (S1–S6).
source: Each Nav α subunit comprises four homologous domains (DI–DIV) with six transmembrane spanning segments (S1–S6) (Noda et al., 1984).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Noda et al., 1984.

claim: The S1–S4 segments in each domain form the four voltage sensing domains (VSDs) that activate on membrane depolarization.
source: The S1–S4 segments in each domain form the four voltage sensing domains (VSDs) that activate on membrane depolarization (Noda et al., 1984; Guy and Seetharamulu, 1986), resulting in channel opening and Na+ influx.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Noda et al., 1984 and Guy and Seetharamulu, 1986.

claim: Nav channels conduct Na+ when the VSDs of domains I, II, and III move outwardly to an activated conformation.
source: Nav channels conduct Na+ when the VSDs of domains I, II, and III move outwardly to an activated conformation (Bezanilla, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bezanilla, 2000.

claim: Fast inactivation of Nav channels is mediated by a hydrophobic (IFM) motif in the cytosolic DIII–DIV linker that binds to a site near the pore.
source: Following opening, fast inactivation occurs (Bezanilla and Armstrong, 1977), mediated by a hydrophobic (IFM) motif in the cytosolic DIII–DIV linker that binds to a site near the pore that is revealed on activation of the DIII and DIV VSDs (Bosmans et al., 2008; Capes et al., 2013; Hsu et al., 2017; Cha et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations describing the mechanism of fast inactivation.

claim: Fast inactivation of open Nav channels occurs when all four VSDs are in the outward/activated position.
source: Thus, fast inactivation of open Nav channels occurs when all four VSDs are in the outward/activated position (Capes et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Capes et al., 2013.

claim: If domains I, II, and III are activated and DIV is in the deactivated position, the IFM motif does not bind, resulting in the generation of a non-inactivating or persistent Nav current (INaP) component.
source: If domains I, II, and III are activated and DIV is in the deactivated position, however, the IFM motif does not bind, which results in the generation of a non-inactivating or persistent Nav current (INaP) component (Chanda and Bezanilla, 2002; Horn et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Chanda and Bezanilla, 2002 and Horn et al., 2000.

claim: INaR was first described in isolated, postnatal day 8–14 rat cerebellar Purkinje neurons.
source: An additional Nav current component, that is observed on membrane hyperpolarizations following brief depolarizing voltage steps and referred to as the resurgent component of Nav current (INaR), was first described in isolated, postnatal day 8–14 rat cerebellar Purkinje neurons (Raman and Bean, 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Raman and Bean, 1997.

claim: INaR has been linked to the regulation of the spontaneous firing of action potentials in cerebellar neurons.
source: Although linked to the regulation of the spontaneous firing of action potentials in cerebellar neurons (Raman and Bean, 1997; Raman and Bean, 1999), INaR was subsequently identified in more than 20 types of neurons in the central and peripheral nervous systems, only some of which are spontaneously active (Lewis and Raman, 2014) suggesting that INaR likely plays diverse functional roles in regulating neuronal excitability.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Raman and Bean, 1997 and 1999.

claim: INaR was identified in more than 20 types of neurons in the central and peripheral nervous systems, only some of which are spontaneously active.
source: Although linked to the regulation of the spontaneous firing of action potentials in cerebellar neurons (Raman and Bean, 1997; Raman and Bean, 1999), INaR was subsequently identified in more than 20 types of neurons in the central and peripheral nervous systems, only some of which are spontaneously active (Lewis and Raman, 2014) suggesting that INaR likely plays diverse functional roles in regulating neuronal excitability.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lewis and Raman, 2014.

claim: INaR likely plays diverse functional roles in regulating neuronal excitability.
source: Although linked to the regulation of the spontaneous firing of action potentials in cerebellar neurons (Raman and Bean, 1997; Raman and Bean, 1999), INaR was subsequently identified in more than 20 types of neurons in the central and peripheral nervous systems, only some of which are spontaneously active (Lewis and Raman, 2014) suggesting that INaR likely plays diverse functional roles in regulating neuronal excitability.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that INaR is found in diverse neuron types with different firing properties.

claim: The time- and voltage-dependent properties of INaR are distinct from INaT and INaP.
source: Although flowing through the same Nav channels as the transient (INaT) and persistent (INaP) sodium current components, the time- and voltage-dependent properties of INaR are distinct (Lewis and Raman, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lewis and Raman, 2014.

claim: INaR is revealed on membrane hyperpolarizations presented after brief (~5 ms) depolarizing voltage steps that evoke INaT.
source: In addition to being revealed on membrane hyperpolarizations presented after brief (~5 ms) depolarizing voltage steps that evoke INaT (Khaliq et al., 2003), for example, the time courses of INaR activation and decay are much slower than INaT.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Khaliq et al., 2003.

claim: The time courses of INaR activation and decay are much slower than INaT.
source: In addition to being revealed on membrane hyperpolarizations presented after brief (~5 ms) depolarizing voltage steps that evoke INaT (Khaliq et al., 2003), for example, the time courses of INaR activation and decay are much slower than INaT.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the kinetic properties of INaR.

claim: A Nav channel gating model with two distinct mechanisms contributing to inactivation was proposed: a conventional, fast inactivation mechanism and a second mechanism favored by brief depolarizations in which channels recover from inactivation by passing through an open, conducting state.
source: These experimental observations were interpreted as suggesting a Nav channel gating model with two distinct mechanisms contributing to inactivation: a conventional, fast inactivation mechanism in which channels recover from inactivation without passing through an open conducting state; and, a second mechanism, favored by brief depolarizations, in which channels recover from inactivation by passing through an open, conducting state (Raman and Bean, 2001).
evidence: This is a previously proposed model cited from Raman and Bean, 2001.

claim: The second mechanism was suggested to be consistent with a voltage-dependent process whereby Nav channels, opened on depolarization, are blocked by an endogenous 'blocking' particle that occludes the pore, driving channels into an 'open-blocked' (OB) state.
source: It was further suggested that the second mechanism was consistent with a voltage-dependent process whereby Nav channels, opened on depolarization, are blocked by an endogenous 'blocking' particle that occludes the pore, driving channels into an 'open-blocked' (OB) state (Raman and Bean, 2001).
evidence: This is a previously proposed mechanism cited from Raman and Bean, 2001.

claim: On membrane hyperpolarization, the blocking particle is displaced, and Na+ flows through unblocked/open Nav channels, generating the resurgent Nav current.
source: On subsequent membrane hyperpolarization, the blocking particle is displaced, and Na+ flows through unblocked/open Nav channels, generating the resurgent Nav current (Raman and Bean, 2001).
evidence: This is part of the previously proposed open-blocked mechanism cited from Raman and Bean, 2001.

claim: In the blocking particle model, blocked Nav channels do not inactivate and inactivated channels are not blocked.
source: Importantly, in this gating scheme, blocked Nav channels do not inactivate and inactivated channels are not blocked, that is, a Nav channel cannot be blocked and inactivated simultaneously (Lewis and Raman, 2014).
evidence: This is a key feature of the previously proposed model cited from Lewis and Raman, 2014.

claim: Proteases (e.g., trypsin/chymotrypsin) that act at positively charged and aromatic/hydrophobic amino acid residues eliminate INaR, while increasing INaT.
source: Studies focused on defining the molecular mechanism(s) underlying the generation of INaR revealed that proteases (e.g., trypsin/chymotrypsin) that act at positively charged and aromatic/hydrophobic amino acid residues eliminate INaR, while increasing INaT, observations interpreted as supporting the blocking particle model and suggesting that the putative blocker was a protein within the Nav channel complex (Grieco et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Grieco et al., 2002.

claim: The transmembrane accessory Navβ4 subunit has a short cytosolic tail with several positive charges and multiple aromatic/hydrophobic residues.
source: Attention focused quickly on the transmembrane accessory Navβ4 subunit, which has a short cytosolic tail with several positive charges and multiple aromatic/hydrophobic residues (Grieco et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Grieco et al., 2005.

claim: Intracellular application of a synthetic Navβ4 peptide containing the tail sequence (β4154–167), following elimination of the resurgent Nav current by trypsin or chymotrypsin, rescued INaR in isolated cerebellar Purkinje neurons.
source: Clear support for a role for Navβ4 was provided in experiments in which intracellular application of a synthetic Navβ4 peptide containing the tail sequence (β4154–167), following elimination of the resurgent Nav current by trypsin or chymotrypsin, rescued INaR in isolated cerebellar Purkinje neurons (Grieco et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Grieco et al., 2005.

claim: Application of the β4154–167 peptide generated resurgent Nav currents in CA3 pyramidal neurons, which lack INaR and Navβ4.
source: In addition, experiments on CA3 pyramidal neurons, which lack INaR and Navβ4, demonstrated that the application of the β4154–167 peptide generated resurgent Nav currents (Grieco et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Grieco et al., 2005.

claim: Treatment of mouse cerebellar granule neurons with small interfering RNAs (siRNAs) targeting Scn4b (Navβ4) resulted in the loss of INaR.
source: Further support for a critical role for Navβ4 was provided with the demonstration that treatment of mouse cerebellar granule neurons with small interfering RNAs (siRNAs) targeting Scn4b (Navβ4) resulted in the loss of INaR and that the subsequent exposure of Scn4b-siRNA-treated cells to the β4154–167 peptide rescued INaR (Grieco et al., 2005; Bant and Raman, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Grieco et al., 2005 and Bant and Raman, 2010.

claim: Exposure of Scn4b-siRNA-treated cells to the β4154–167 peptide rescued INaR.
source: Further support for a critical role for Navβ4 was provided with the demonstration that treatment of mouse cerebellar granule neurons with small interfering RNAs (siRNAs) targeting Scn4b (Navβ4) resulted in the loss of INaR and that the subsequent exposure of Scn4b-siRNA-treated cells to the β4154–167 peptide rescued INaR (Grieco et al., 2005; Bant and Raman, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Grieco et al., 2005 and Bant and Raman, 2010.

claim: INaR was reduced (by ~50%), but not eliminated, in cerebellar Purkinje neurons in (Scn4b-/-) mice lacking Navβ4.
source: In experiments designed to test directly the hypothesis that Navβ4 is required for the generation of INaR, however, we found that INaR was reduced (by ~50%), but not eliminated, and that the time- and voltage-dependent properties of the currents were unaffected in cerebellar Purkinje neurons in (Scn4b-/-) mice lacking Navβ4 (Ransdell et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ransdell et al., 2017.

claim: The time- and voltage-dependent properties of INaR were unaffected in cerebellar Purkinje neurons in (Scn4b-/-) mice lacking Navβ4.
source: In experiments designed to test directly the hypothesis that Navβ4 is required for the generation of INaR, however, we found that INaR was reduced (by ~50%), but not eliminated, and that the time- and voltage-dependent properties of the currents were unaffected in cerebellar Purkinje neurons in (Scn4b-/-) mice lacking Navβ4 (Ransdell et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ransdell et al., 2017.

claim: INaR is readily measured in Scn4b-/- striatal neurons.
source: In addition, it has been reported that INaR is readily measured in Scn4b-/- striatal neurons (Miyazaki et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Miyazaki et al., 2014.

claim: Additional mechanisms beyond Navβ4 contribute to the generation of INaR.
source: These observations clearly suggest that additional mechanisms contribute to the generation of INaR.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that INaR persists in the absence of Navβ4.

claim: INaR is decreased in neonatal mouse cerebellar Purkinje neurons isolated from animals harboring a targeted disruption in the Fgf14 locus.
source: Support for this hypothesis was provided in studies showing that INaR is decreased in neonatal mouse cerebellar Purkinje neurons isolated from animals harboring a targeted disruption in the Fgf14 (which encodes intracellular fibroblast growth factor 14 [iFGF14]) locus (White et al., 2019), as well as in wild type neonatal Purkinje cells following exposure to an interfering RNA targeting the Fgf14b variant (Yan et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to White et al., 2019 and Yan et al., 2014.

claim: INaR is decreased in wild type neonatal Purkinje cells following exposure to an interfering RNA targeting the Fgf14b variant.
source: Support for this hypothesis was provided in studies showing that INaR is decreased in neonatal mouse cerebellar Purkinje neurons isolated from animals harboring a targeted disruption in the Fgf14 (which encodes intracellular fibroblast growth factor 14 [iFGF14]) locus (White et al., 2019), as well as in wild type neonatal Purkinje cells following exposure to an interfering RNA targeting the Fgf14b variant (Yan et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Yan et al., 2014.

claim: INaR was readily detected in Purkinje neurons isolated from neonatal animals lacking both Scn4b and Fgf14.
source: Interestingly, however, it was also reported that INaR was readily detected in Purkinje neurons isolated from neonatal animals lacking both Scn4b and Fgf14 (White et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to White et al., 2019.

claim: The maximal amplitude of INaR is observed at approximately –45 mV.
source: The maximal amplitude of INaR is observed at approximately –45 mV (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Prolonging the duration of the +20 mV depolarizing voltage step resulted in the marked attenuation of the peak amplitudes of INaR measured during hyperpolarizing voltage steps to –45 mV.
source: These experiments revealed that prolonging the duration of the +20 mV depolarizing voltage step resulted in the marked attenuation of the peak amplitudes of INaR measured during hyperpolarizing voltage steps to –45 mV (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The time course of the attenuation of INaR was well described by a single exponential characterized by a mean ± SEM (n = 12) time constant of 15.5 ± 0.5 ms.
source: The time course of the attenuation of INaR was well described by a single exponential characterized by a mean ± SEM (n = 12) time constant of 15.5 ± 0.5 ms (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The attenuation of INaR as a function of the duration of the depolarizing voltage step occurs independent of the direction (inward versus outward) of Na+ flux during the depolarizing voltage step.
source: Under these conditions, depolarizing voltage steps to +46 mV evoked outward INaT. Peak INaR amplitudes, revealed during hyperpolarizing voltage steps to –45 mV, however, were also found to vary as a function of the duration of the depolarizing voltage step, revealing that INaR and the time-dependent attenuation of INaR are not affected by the direction (inward versus outward) of Na+ flux during the depolarizing voltage step.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Under conditions where INaT is outward, the time course of the attenuation of INaR was well described by a single exponential with a mean ± SEM (n = 6) time constant of 13.8 ± 1.1 ms.
source: As is evident from the representative records and the plot of normalized peak INaR amplitudes (on the right), the attenuation of INaR as a function of the duration of the depolarizing voltage steps to +46 mV is also well described by a single exponential with a mean ± SEM time constant of 13.8 ± 1.1 ms (n = 6), a value similar to that observed when INaT was inward (B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Following brief depolarizations, there is a time-dependent accumulation of Nav channels (which underlie INaR) in a non-conducting state, and this accumulation occurs independent of the direction of the movement of permeating Na+ ions.
source: Taken together, these combined results demonstrate that, following brief depolarizations, there is a time-dependent accumulation of Nav channels (which underlie INaR) in a non-conducting state, and that this accumulation occurs independent of the direction of the movement of permeating Na+ ions.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data in Figure 2.

claim: Hyperpolarizations to –45 mV following brief (5 ms) depolarizations to various membrane potentials (ranging from –45 to +10 mV) resulted in identical INaR amplitudes.
source: These experiments revealed that hyperpolarizations to –45 mV following brief (5 ms) depolarizations to various membrane potentials (ranging from –45 to +10 mV) resulted in identical INaR amplitudes (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Varying the voltage of the depolarizing step did not affect the kinetics of the decay of INaR.
source: Additionally, varying the voltage of the depolarizing step did not affect the kinetics of the decay of INaR (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The opening of Nav channels that conduct INaR is not affected by the voltage of the prior membrane depolarization.
source: The opening of Nav channels that conduct INaR, therefore, is not affected by the voltage of the prior membrane depolarization.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data in Figure 2D-F.

claim: There are two parallel, and kinetically distinct, Nav channel inactivation pathways: a fast inactivating pathway that is responsible for INaT; and, a second, slower inactivation pathway that underlies INaR.
source: Taken together, these observations suggest that there are two parallel, and kinetically distinct, Nav channel inactivation pathways: a fast inactivating pathway that is responsible for INaT; and, a second, slower inactivation pathway that underlies INaR.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations.

claim: The optimized Markov model includes parallel fast (IF1, IF2) and slow inactivation (IS) pathways.
source: The optimized Markov model (Figure 3A) includes parallel fast (IF1, IF2) and slow inactivation (IS) pathways to reconcile the experimental findings (Figure 2) that the duration of the depolarizing voltage step that underlie Nav channel activation, and not the potential of the depolarizing voltage step or the direction (i.e., inward or outward) of the Na+ flux through open channels, determines the amplitudes of INaR recorded during subsequent membrane hyperpolarizations.
evidence: This is a description of the model structure shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The model successfully reproduces the observed, time-dependent attenuation of peak INaR amplitudes that is evident experimentally on membrane hyperpolarizations following depolarizing voltage steps of varying durations.
source: The model successfully reproduces the observed, time-dependent attenuation of peak INaR amplitudes that is evident experimentally on membrane hyperpolarizations following depolarizing voltage steps of varying durations (H), and the finding that the peak amplitude of INaR is not affected by the potential of the depolarizing voltage step (I).
evidence: This is supported by modeling results shown in Figure 3H.

claim: The model reproduces the finding that the peak amplitude of INaR is not affected by the potential of the depolarizing voltage step.
source: The model successfully reproduces the observed, time-dependent attenuation of peak INaR amplitudes that is evident experimentally on membrane hyperpolarizations following depolarizing voltage steps of varying durations (H), and the finding that the peak amplitude of INaR is not affected by the potential of the depolarizing voltage step (I).
evidence: This is supported by modeling results shown in Figure 3I.

claim: Fast inactivation of INaT (during the 0 mV step) reflects (simulated) channels exiting the open state and accumulating into the IF1/IF2 states.
source: As illustrated, fast inactivation of INaT (during the 0 mV step) reflects (simulated) channels exiting the open state and accumulating into the IF1/IF2 states.
evidence: This is supported by the gating state occupancy plot in Figure 4.

claim: The activation of INaR (at –45 mV) reflects channel transitioning from IF1/IF2 back into the open state.
source: The activation of INaR (at –45 mV) reflects channel transitioning from IF1/IF2 back into the open state, and the decay of INaR during the –45 mV step reflects the time-dependent accumulation of (simulated) Nav channels in the secondary, slow-inactivated state, IS (see Figures 3A and 4A).
evidence: This is supported by the gating state occupancy plot in Figure 4.

claim: The decay of INaR during the –45 mV step reflects the time-dependent accumulation of (simulated) Nav channels in the secondary, slow-inactivated state, IS.
source: The activation of INaR (at –45 mV) reflects channel transitioning from IF1/IF2 back into the open state, and the decay of INaR during the –45 mV step reflects the time-dependent accumulation of (simulated) Nav channels in the secondary, slow-inactivated state, IS (see Figures 3A and 4A).
evidence: This is supported by the gating state occupancy plot in Figure 4.

claim: The distinct pathways of inactivation are separated in time, but are not distinguished by differing voltage dependences.
source: The distinct pathways of inactivation are separated in time, but are not distinguished by differing voltage dependences.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the model simulations.

claim: When the time interval at –90 mV was reduced to 20 ms, the amplitude of INaR was reduced to a greater extent than the amplitude of INaT.
source: As illustrated in the representative records shown in Figure 5A, this voltage-clamp paradigm revealed that, when the time interval at –90 mV was reduced to 20 ms, the amplitude of INaR was indeed reduced to a greater extent than the amplitude of INaT.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The 20 ms hyperpolarizing voltage step to –90 mV was sufficient to provide nearly complete (0.95 ± 0.01; n = 6) recovery of INaT.
source: Plotting the relative peak amplitudes of INaT and INaR measured during the second protocol, compared with the first, reveals that the 20 ms hyperpolarizing voltage step to –90 mV was sufficient to provide nearly complete (0.95 ± 0.01; n = 6) recovery of INaT (Figure 5B), whereas there was a marked reduction in the amplitude of INaR (0.63 ± 0.05; n = 6), measured during the second, compared with the first, protocol (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: There was a marked reduction in the amplitude of INaR (0.63 ± 0.05; n = 6), measured during the second, compared with the first, protocol.
source: Plotting the relative peak amplitudes of INaT and INaR measured during the second protocol, compared with the first, reveals that the 20 ms hyperpolarizing voltage step to –90 mV was sufficient to provide nearly complete (0.95 ± 0.01; n = 6) recovery of INaT (Figure 5B), whereas there was a marked reduction in the amplitude of INaR (0.63 ± 0.05; n = 6), measured during the second, compared with the first, protocol (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Nav channels open during membrane hyperpolarizations from depolarized potentials and these (open) channels recover from inactivation at a rate that is distinct from the complement of Nav channels responsible for INaT.
source: The results presented in Figure 5 indicate that Nav channels open during membrane hyperpolarizations from depolarized potentials and that these (open) channels recover from inactivation at a rate that is distinct from the complement of Nav channels responsible for INaT.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data in Figure 5.

claim: The voltage dependences and the magnitudes of the Nav currents recorded using the three voltage-clamp protocols (depolarizing ramp, hyperpolarizing ramp, and steady-state voltage step) are indistinguishable.
source: As is evident, the voltage dependences and the magnitudes of the Nav currents recorded using the three voltage-clamp protocols (in the same cell) are indeed indistinguishable.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The previously proposed model of Nav channel gating in mouse cerebellar Purkinje neurons involves two distinct competing pathways that depopulate the open state: fast Nav channel inactivation and blockade of open Nav channels.
source: In this earlier model (illustrated in Figure 7A), there are two distinct competing pathways that depopulate the open state, one of which involves fast Nav channel inactivation and results in the population of the I6 state (Figure 7A) and the other, competing, pathway involves the blockade of open Nav channels and the generation of the OB state (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is a description of the previously proposed model shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The isolation of the OB state from all of the other kinetic states except the open state is a distinctive feature in the model of Raman and Bean.
source: The isolation of the OB state from all of the other kinetic states except the open state is a distinctive feature in the model of Raman and Bean (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is a description of a key feature of the Raman and Bean model.

claim: In the Raman and Bean model, channels that have entered the OB state can only exit this state by transitioning into the open/conducting state to generate resurgent Na+ influx.
source: This configuration means that channels that have entered the OB state can only exit this state (i.e., become unblocked) by transitioning into the open/conducting state to generate resurgent Na+ influx, that is, INaR (Raman and Bean, 2001).
evidence: This is a description of the mechanism in the Raman and Bean model.

claim: The open channel block model recapitulates the voltage and time dependences of INaT activation, inactivation and recovery from inactivation in mouse cerebellar Purkinje neurons.
source: Additional simulations revealed that this model also recapitulates the voltage and time dependences of INaT activation, inactivation and recovery from inactivation (Figure 7C–E) in mouse cerebellar Purkinje neurons, although the modeled INaT activates at more hyperpolarized voltages than native INaT.
evidence: This is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 7C-E.

claim: The open channel block model predicts that the magnitude of INaR evoked at all hyperpolarized membrane potentials, relative to the peak amplitude of INaT (evoked at 0 mV), is much smaller than observed experimentally.
source: Although recapitulating the voltage dependence of INaR activation (Figure 7F), the model also predicts that the magnitude of INaR evoked at all hyperpolarized membrane potentials, relative to the peak amplitude of INaT (evoked at 0 mV), is much smaller than observed experimentally (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 7F.

claim: In the open-channel block model of INaR gating, more positive depolarizing voltage steps promote entry into the OB state, whereas channels are favored to undergo fast (conventional) inactivation at more hyperpolarized membrane potentials.
source: In the open-channel block model of INaR gating (Figure 7A), more positive depolarizing voltage steps promote entry into the OB state, whereas channels are favored to undergo fast (conventional) inactivation at more hyperpolarized membrane potentials (Raman and Bean, 2001; Lewis and Raman, 2014).
evidence: This is a description of the voltage-dependent behavior in the open-channel block model.

claim: Increasing the duration of the brief (5 ms) depolarizing voltage step (to 0 mV) in the open channel block model resulted in very little time-dependent attenuation of the amplitude of INaR recorded on membrane hyperpolarization to –45 mV.
source: In contrast to what is observed experimentally (Figure 2), for example, increasing the duration of the brief (5 ms) depolarizing voltage step (to 0 mV) in the open channel block model resulted in very little time-dependent attenuation of the amplitude of INaR recorded on membrane hyperpolarization to –45 mV (Figure 7G and H).
evidence: This is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 7G and H.

claim: The time course of the decay of the resurgent currents predicted by the open channel block model are slower than observed experimentally for INaR in mouse cerebellar Purkinje neurons.
source: In addition, the time course of the decay of the resurgent currents predicted by the open channel block model (Figure 7A) are slower than we observed experimentally for INaR in mouse cerebellar Purkinje neurons (Figure 7I).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of simulation results (Figure 7I) with experimental data.

claim: INaR waveforms evoked using a single (80 ms) hyperpolarizing voltage step to –45 mV and INaR recorded at –45 mV during successive brief (2 ms) hyperpolarizing voltage steps interspersed with brief (5 ms) depolarizations to 0 mV were quite similar.
source: As is evident in the experimental records shown in Figure 8A, however, INaR waveforms evoked (in the same cell) using these two voltage-clamp protocols were quite similar.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: The envelope of the currents generated using the two protocols (single sustained hyperpolarization vs. repeated brief hyperpolarizations) superimpose, suggesting that the inactivation pathway responsible for INaR decay does not compete with fast inactivation.
source: As is evident (A), the envelope of the currents generated using these two protocols superimpose, suggesting that the inactivation pathway responsible for INaR decay does not compete with fast inactivation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data in Figure 8A.

claim: The novel kinetic state model reproduces the Nav currents recorded from a Purkinje neuron that is depolarized (to 0 mV) and repolarized (to –45 mV) repeatedly.
source: The representative traces presented in Figure 8A were recapitulated in simulations (Figure 8B) using the novel gating state model (Figure 3A) developed here.
evidence: This is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 8B.

claim: The Raman-Bean model does not reproduce the Nav currents recorded from a Purkinje neuron that is depolarized (to 0 mV) and repolarized (to –45 mV) repeatedly.
source: This voltage-clamp protocol was also applied in simulations using the previously described (Figure 7A) open channel block model (Raman and Bean, 2001). In this case, in marked contrast with the results presented in Figure 8, the model does not reproduce the experimental data (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The targeted deletion of Scn4b in mice results in a marked (~50%) reduction in INaR amplitudes in cerebellar Purkinje neurons without measurable effects on INaR kinetics or voltage dependence.
source: We previously reported that the targeted deletion of Scn4b in mice results in a marked (~50%) reduction in INaR amplitudes in cerebellar Purkinje neurons (Figure 9A) without measurable effects on INaR kinetics or voltage dependence (Ransdell et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ransdell et al., 2017 and data shown in Figure 9A.

claim: The attenuation of the amplitude of INaR in the Scn4b-/- model is the result of the reduced accumulation of channels in the IF2 state during the initial depolarization and increased occupancy in the IS state.
source: The gating state occupancy plots (Figure 9D) reveal that the attenuation of the amplitude of INaR in the Scn4b-/- model is the result of the reduced accumulation of channels in the IF2 state during the initial depolarization and increased occupancy in the IS state.
evidence: This is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 9D.

claim: Navβ4 delays entry into the slow-inactivated state (IS), allowing for greater recovery from conventional inactivation and thus, larger INaR amplitudes.
source: Together, these data suggest that Navβ4 delays entry into the slow-inactivated state (IS), allowing for greater recovery from conventional inactivation and thus, larger INaR amplitudes (see Discussion).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the modeling results.

claim: The model developed here accounts for the experimental finding that the peak amplitude of INaR is sensitive to the duration of the preceding depolarizing voltage step, with longer depolarizations resulting in lower INaR amplitudes.
source: The model, for example, accounts for the experimental finding that the peak amplitude of INaR (recorded on membrane hyperpolarizations following brief depolarizations that evoke INaT) is sensitive to the duration of the preceding depolarizing voltage step, with longer depolarizations resulting in lower INaR amplitudes.
evidence: This is a summary of how the model accounts for experimental observations.

claim: The dependence of INaR amplitudes on the duration of the depolarizing voltage step was observed when the inward driving force of Na+ was reduced or eliminated.
source: Importantly, the dependence of INaR amplitudes on the duration of the depolarizing voltage step was also observed when the inward driving force of Na+ was reduced or eliminated.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The model reproduces the experimental finding that INaR amplitudes are not dependent on the voltage of the initial depolarizing voltage step (that evokes INaT).
source: In addition, the model reproduces the experimental finding that INaR amplitudes are not dependent on the voltage of the initial depolarizing voltage step (that evokes INaT).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D-E and modeling results in Figure 3I.

claim: The voltage dependence of INaR (revealed on membrane hyperpolarizations) mirrors the voltage dependence of INaP.
source: Finally, and also consistent with the experimental data, the voltage dependence of INaR (revealed on membrane hyperpolarizations) mirrors the voltage dependence of INaP (see Figure 6).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The voltage dependence of INaP is identical to the voltage dependence of INaR.
source: Interestingly, this last observation, that is, that the voltage dependence of INaP is identical to the voltage dependence of INaR, was previously reported (Kay et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kay et al., 1998.

claim: In the open-channel block model, a blocking particle occludes the Nav channel pore that is opened on membrane depolarization, functionally competing with conventional, fast inactivation.
source: In this earlier model (Figure 7A) of INaR gating, a blocking particle occludes the Nav channel pore that is opened on membrane depolarization, functionally competing with conventional, fast inactivation, and, in addition, the OB state is isolated off the open/conducting state (Raman and Bean, 2001).
evidence: This is a description of the mechanism in the Raman and Bean model.

claim: In the open-channel block model, entry into the OB state is promoted by membrane depolarizations to positive potentials.
source: In this model, entry into the OB state is promoted by membrane depolarizations to positive potentials and, on subsequent membrane hyperpolarization, the blocking particle is expelled by the Na+ driven through the unblocked Nav channel pore (Aman and Raman, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Aman and Raman, 2010.

claim: In the open-channel block model, on membrane hyperpolarization, the blocking particle is expelled by the Na+ driven through the unblocked Nav channel pore.
source: In this model, entry into the OB state is promoted by membrane depolarizations to positive potentials and, on subsequent membrane hyperpolarization, the blocking particle is expelled by the Na+ driven through the unblocked Nav channel pore (Aman and Raman, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Aman and Raman, 2010.

claim: In the open-channel block model, the larger the driving force on Na+, the more rapidly the blocker is displaced.
source: In addition, the larger the driving force on Na+, the more rapidly the blocker is displaced (Aman and Raman, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Aman and Raman, 2010.

claim: The peak amplitude of INaR is observed at relatively hyperpolarized (−45 to –30 mV) membrane potentials.
source: This process, while intrinsically voltage-independent, therefore, is tied to the driving force on Na+, consistent with the experimental observation that the peak amplitude of INaR is observed at relatively hyperpolarized (−45 to –30 mV) membrane potentials (Aman and Raman, 2010; Lewis and Raman, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Aman and Raman, 2010 and Lewis and Raman, 2014.

claim: At more negative membrane potentials, closed state inactivation begins to dominate, and INaR is reduced.
source: At more negative membrane potentials, closed state inactivation begins to dominate, and INaR is reduced (Raman and Bean, 2001; Lewis and Raman, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Raman and Bean, 2001 and Lewis and Raman, 2014.

claim: The magnitude of INaR is substantially reduced when the initial depolarizing voltage step is increased in duration.
source: The finding that the magnitude of INaR is substantially reduced when the initial depolarizing voltage step is increased in duration was previously reported (Raman and Bean, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Raman and Bean, 2001.

claim: The time-dependent accumulation of Nav channels into the slow-inactivated state occurs independent of the direction of the movement of permeating Na+ ions.
source: In addition, experimental results presented here demonstrate that the time-dependent accumulation of Nav channels into the slow-inactivated state occurs independent of the direction of the movement of permeating Na+ ions.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: INaR reflects the transitioning of Nav channels that have undergone conventional fast inactivation, into an open/conducting state on membrane hyperpolarizations.
source: The experiments and the simulations presented here suggest that INaR reflects the transitioning of Nav channels that have undergone conventional fast inactivation, into an open/conducting state on membrane hyperpolarizations.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experimental and modeling data.

claim: The model includes two parallel, but distinct, inactivation pathways: the fast (i.e., IF1 and IF2) inactivation pathway and the slow (i.e., IS) inactivation pathway.
source: Consistent with the slow decay of INaR, the model includes two parallel, but distinct, inactivation pathways: the fast (i.e., IF1 and IF2) inactivation pathway and the slow (i.e., IS) inactivation pathway, which satisfies the key experimental finding that the amplitude of INaR is insensitive to the voltage of the initial depolarization (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a description of the model structure.

claim: The slower component of the biexponential decay of INaT (measured at –30 mV) in Purkinje neurons is identical to the decay rate of INaR (also measured at –30 mV).
source: Although it was previously reported that the slower component of the biexponential decay of INaT (measured at –30 mV) in Purkinje neurons is identical to the decay rate of INaR (also measured at –30 mV), this observation was interpreted as suggesting that all Nav channels initially undergo open channel block (Raman and Bean, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Raman and Bean, 2001.

claim: There is still a time-dependent attenuation of INaR amplitudes on membrane hyperpolarizations following depolarizations to positive membrane potentials, with little or no inward driving force on Na+.
source: In the experiments here, we found that there is still a time-dependent attenuation of INaR amplitudes on membrane hyperpolarizations following depolarizations to positive membrane potentials, with little or no inward driving force on Na+.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: These findings are inconsistent with the open-channel block hypothesis, in which positive membrane potentials are thought to promote and stabilize open-channel block.
source: These findings are inconsistent with the open-channel block hypothesis, in which positive membrane potentials are thought to promote and stabilize open-channel block (Raman and Bean, 2001; Aman and Raman, 2010; Lewis and Raman, 2014).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: One assumption usually made when considering the gating of Nav channels is that deactivation must occur prior to recovery from inactivation.
source: One assumption usually made when considering the gating of Nav channels is that deactivation must occur prior to recovery from inactivation.
evidence: This is stated as a common assumption in the field.

claim: Nav channels cannot exit the conventional inactivated state directly into an open or conducting state.
source: Or, to state another way, Nav channels cannot exit the conventional inactivated state directly into an open or conducting state.
evidence: This is stated as a common assumption in the field.

claim: Recovery from inactivation occurs with a delay and is voltage-dependent in CA1 hippocampal neurons and the squid giant axon.
source: This idea is based on voltage-clamp experiments conducted on CA1 hippocampal neurons (Kuo and Bean, 1994) and the squid giant axon (Armstrong, 2006), which revealed that recovery from inactivation occurs with a delay and is voltage-dependent.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kuo and Bean, 1994 and Armstrong, 2006.

claim: If deactivation of VSD IV is sufficient to release the cytosolic DIII–DIV linker peptide from the channel pore, while VSD I, II, and III remain in the activated conformation, Nav channels could transit from an inactivated state directly into an open/conducting state.
source: However, if deactivation of VSD IV is sufficient to release the cytosolic DIII–DIV linker peptide from the channel pore, while VSD I, II, and III remain in the activated conformation, Nav channels could transit from an inactivated state directly into an open/conducting state.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed to explain the mechanism of INaR generation.

claim: Scorpion beta toxins induce INaR in heterologously (in HEK-293 cells) expressed Nav channels.
source: Schiavon et al., 2012, for example, demonstrated that scorpion beta toxins induce INaR in heterologously (in HEK-293 cells) expressed Nav channels.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Schiavon et al., 2012.

claim: Scorpion beta toxins cause a negative shift in the voltage dependence of DI-VSD, DII-VSD, and DIII-VSD activation by trapping the DII-VSD in the activated position after depolarizing prepulses.
source: These toxins were previously shown to cause a negative shift in the voltage dependence of DI-VSD, DII-VSD, and DIII-VSD activation by trapping the DII-VSD in the activated position after depolarizing prepulses (Cestèle et al., 1998; Schiavon et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Cestèle et al., 1998 and Schiavon et al., 2006.

claim: Resurgent Nav currents have been induced in heterologously expressed (in HEK-293 cells) Nav1.5-encoded channels following application of the classical type II pyrethroid, deltamethrin.
source: Resurgent Nav currents have also been induced in heterologously expressed (in HEK-293 cells) Nav1.5-encoded channels following application of the classical type II pyrethroid, deltamethrin.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Thull et al., 2020.

claim: Deltamethrin-modified Nav1.5 channels recover from inactivation prior to deactivation.
source: Similar to our model for the generation of INaR, the deltamethrin-modified Nav1.5 channels were found to recover from inactivation prior to deactivation (Thull et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Thull et al., 2020.

claim: Heterologously expressed mutant Nav1.7-encoded channels have prolonged deactivation time constants at the hyperpolarized membrane potentials associated with the activation of INaR.
source: In addition, it has also been reported (Cummins et al., 2004) that heterologously expressed (in HEK-293 cells) mutant Nav1.7-encoded channels have prolonged deactivation time constants at the hyperpolarized membrane potentials associated with the activation of INaR.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Cummins et al., 2004.

claim: Mutant Nav1.7 channels display an increase in the relative amplitude of the non-inactivating Nav current (i.e., INaP).
source: These mutant Nav1.7 channels were also reported to display an increase in the relative amplitude of the non-inactivating Nav current (i.e., INaP).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Cummins et al., 2004.

claim: Two fast-inactivated states, that is, IF1 and IF2, were required to recapitulate the experimental data.
source: In developing the model (Figure 3A), we found that two fast-inactivated states, that is, IF1 and IF2, were required to recapitulate the experimental data.
evidence: This is a description of the model development process.

claim: The model was initially developed with two slow-inactivated states (IS, IS2) for symmetry, but the two slow-inactivated states were redundant.
source: We also note here that, initially, the model was developed with two slow-inactivated states (IS, IS2) for symmetry. The simulations revealed, however, that the two slow-inactivated states were redundant and that we were able to fit the experimental data reliably with only one of these slow-inactivated states.
evidence: This is a description of the model development process.

claim: The model topology and rate constants, while reliably recapitulating the time- and voltage-dependent properties of the currents determined experimentally, are not necessarily 'unique' or potentially the 'most simple'.
source: It is important to note that we appreciate that our model topology and rate constants, while reliably recapitulating the time- and voltage-dependent properties of the currents determined experimentally, are not necessarily 'unique' or potentially the 'most simple'.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of the limitations of Markov modeling.

claim: In using Markov kinetic state modeling, it is not possible to tell the uniqueness or the ambiguity of the model (both with regard to the parameters and the model topology).
source: Indeed, in using Markov kinetic state modeling, it is not possible to tell the uniqueness or the ambiguity of the model (both with regard to the parameters and the model topology).
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of the limitations of Markov modeling.

claim: There are many model structures and parameter sets that can adequately fit some experimental datasets.
source: These efforts revealed that there are many model structures and parameter sets that can adequately fit some experimental datasets.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Mangold et al., 2021.

claim: The targeted deletion of Scn8a (which encodes the Nav1.6 α subunit) in mouse cerebellar Purkinje neurons resulted in a 90% reduction in the amplitude of INaR.
source: Soon after the discovery of INaR, it was reported that the targeted deletion of Scn8a (which encodes the Nav1.6 α subunit) in mouse cerebellar Purkinje neurons resulted in a 90% reduction in the amplitude of INaR, suggesting that, of the α subunits (Nav1.1 and Nav1.6) expressed in Purkinje neurons (Vega-Saenz de Miera et al., 1997; Xiao et al., 2013), Nav channels formed by Nav1.6 are the major contributors to INaR (Raman et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Raman et al., 1997.

claim: Nav channels formed by Nav1.6 are the major contributors to INaR in cerebellar Purkinje neurons.
source: Soon after the discovery of INaR, it was reported that the targeted deletion of Scn8a (which encodes the Nav1.6 α subunit) in mouse cerebellar Purkinje neurons resulted in a 90% reduction in the amplitude of INaR, suggesting that, of the α subunits (Nav1.1 and Nav1.6) expressed in Purkinje neurons (Vega-Saenz de Miera et al., 1997; Xiao et al., 2013), Nav channels formed by Nav1.6 are the major contributors to INaR (Raman et al., 1997).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that deletion of Nav1.6 reduces INaR by 90%.

claim: The targeted deletion of Scn1a (which encodes the Nav1.1 α subunit) results in ~65% reduction in INaR.
source: However, it was later reported that the targeted deletion of Scn1a (which encodes the Nav1.1 α subunit) also results in ~65% reduction in INaR, suggesting that multiple Nav α subunits contribute to INaR in cerebellar Purkinje neurons and, in addition, that the contributions are non-linear.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from previous research.

claim: Multiple Nav α subunits contribute to INaR in cerebellar Purkinje neurons and the contributions are non-linear.
source: However, it was later reported that the targeted deletion of Scn1a (which encodes the Nav1.1 α subunit) also results in ~65% reduction in INaR, suggesting that multiple Nav α subunits contribute to INaR in cerebellar Purkinje neurons and, in addition, that the contributions are non-linear.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that deletion of either Nav1.1 or Nav1.6 reduces INaR substantially.

claim: All but one (Nav1.3) of the nine Nav channel α subunits have been shown to mediate, or can be induced to mediate, INaR in native or heterologous cells.
source: To date, all but one (Nav1.3) of the nine Nav channel α subunits have been shown to mediate, or can be induced to mediate, INaR in native or heterologous cells (Lewis and Raman, 2014; Jarecki et al., 2010, Do and Bean, 2004; Tan et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: In the model proposed here, the amplitude of INaR is dependent on the proportion of Nav channels that are non-inactivating at hyperpolarized voltages and the proportion of these non-inactivating channels that accumulate into a slow-inactivated state.
source: In the model proposed here, the amplitude of INaR is dependent on, and ultimately regulated by, two factors: the proportion of Nav channels that are non-inactivating at hyperpolarized voltages, that is, the number of channels that recover from inactivation into an open state on repolarization; and, the proportion of these non-inactivating channels that accumulate into a slow-inactivated state.
evidence: This is a description of the key factors regulating INaR amplitude in the model.

claim: Navβ4 expression regulates INaR by influencing slow inactivation.
source: In the simulations presented in Figure 9, we show that by promoting the occupancy of the IS (slow-inactivated) state, we can recapitulate the experimental observation that INaR amplitudes are reduced in Scn4b-/-, compared with wild type, cerebellar Purkinje neurons, suggesting the possibility that Navβ4 expression regulates INaR by influencing slow inactivation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the modeling results in Figure 9.

claim: Mutations in the Nav1.6 and Nav1.7 α subunits that enhance or inhibit slow inactivation result in reduced or increased, respectively, INaR amplitudes.
source: The hypothesis that INaR is directly affected by Nav channel slow inactivation is also consistent with previous work (Hampl et al., 2016), showing that mutations in the Nav1.6 and Nav1.7 α subunits that enhance or inhibit slow inactivation also result in reduced or increased, respectively, INaR amplitudes.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hampl et al., 2016.

claim: Mutation of the IFM motif (to QQQ) in Nav1.4, in addition to completely eliminating fast inactivation, increases the proportion of channels that enter the slow inactivated state.
source: Interestingly, it has also been reported that mutation of the IFM motif (to QQQ) in Nav1.4, in addition to completely eliminating fast inactivation, increases the proportion of channels that enter the slow inactivated state (Featherstone et al., 1996), suggesting that the model developed here (Figure 3A) in which the fast and slow components of inactivation are exclusive, may be applicable to diverse Nav channels in different cell types and encoded by different α subunits.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Featherstone et al., 1996.

claim: The model developed here in which the fast and slow components of inactivation are exclusive, may be applicable to diverse Nav channels in different cell types and encoded by different α subunits.
source: Interestingly, it has also been reported that mutation of the IFM motif (to QQQ) in Nav1.4, in addition to completely eliminating fast inactivation, increases the proportion of channels that enter the slow inactivated state (Featherstone et al., 1996), suggesting that the model developed here (Figure 3A) in which the fast and slow components of inactivation are exclusive, may be applicable to diverse Nav channels in different cell types and encoded by different α subunits.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observation that the model structure may be generalizable.

claim: There are a number of additional factors, intrinsic and extrinsic, to Nav α subunits, as well as additional pre- and post-translational mechanisms, that regulate persistent Nav currents and slow inactivation.
source: There are a number of additional factors, intrinsic and extrinsic, to Nav α subunits, as well as additional pre- and post-translational mechanisms, that regulate persistent Nav currents (Aman et al., 2009; Hammarstrom and Gage, 1998; Paul et al., 2016; Lin and Baines, 2015) and slow inactivation (Chen et al., 2008; Silva, 2014; Chen et al., 2006; Carr et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: In the model developed here, the combined effects of factors that regulate persistent Nav currents and slow inactivation will regulate/modulate the amplitudes and the time- and voltage-dependent properties of INaR.
source: In the model developed and presented here, the combined effects of these factors/mechanisms will regulate/modulate the amplitudes and the time- and voltage-dependent properties of INaR.
evidence: This is an inference about how the model can account for various regulatory mechanisms.

claim: The Nav channels underlying INaR, compared to the sum of the Nav channels underlying INaT, are differentially sensitive to slow inactivation.
source: In this context, it is interesting to note that the experiments presented in Figure 5 indicate that the Nav channels underlying INaR, compared to the sum of the Nav channels underlying INaT, are differentially sensitive to slow inactivation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data in Figure 5.

claim: There is functional (and perhaps molecular) heterogeneity in the population of Nav channels underlying the Nav currents in mouse cerebellar Purkinje neurons.
source: This observation clearly suggests that there is functional (and perhaps molecular) heterogeneity in the population of Nav channels underlying the Nav currents in mouse cerebellar Purkinje neurons, with channels underlying INaR having properties distinct from at least a portion of the Nav channels that participate in the generation of INaT, but that do not produce INaR.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of differential sensitivity to slow inactivation.

claim: INaR has a greater sensitivity to tetrodotoxin block than INaT in mouse cerebellar Purkinje neurons.
source: This possibility is consistent with results presented by White et al., 2019, in which INaR was found to have a greater sensitivity to tetrodotoxin block than INaT in mouse cerebellar Purkinje neurons.
evidence: This is supported by citation to White et al., 2019.

claim: The Markov model developed here was created to reflect a single channel population, that is, Nav channels capable of generating both INaT and INaR.
source: It should also be noted that the Markov model developed here was created to reflect a single channel population, that is, Nav channels capable of generating both INaT and INaR.
evidence: This is a description of a limitation of the model.

claim: The developed Markov model does not reproduce the differential recovery from inactivation presented in Figure 5.
source: As such, the developed Markov model does not reproduce the differential recovery from inactivation presented in Figure 5.
evidence: This is a description of a limitation of the model.

claim: Two parameters are critical in determining the magnitude and the time- and voltage-dependent properties of INaR: (1) the relative amplitude of the persistent Nav current, INaP, component; and, (2) the proportion of the persistent Nav channels that undergo slow inactivation.
source: Based on the experimental data and the computational modeling presented here, we propose a novel, blocking particle-independent, gating mechanism for the generation of INaR that involves two, kinetically distinct inactivation pathways. The modeling results suggest that two parameters are critical in determining the magnitude and the time- and voltage-dependent properties of INaR: (1) the relative amplitude of the persistent Nav current, INaP, component; and, (2) the proportion of the persistent Nav channels (channels that fail to undergo fast inactivation) that undergo slow inactivation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the modeling results.

claim: INaR has been identified in over 20 types of neurons, many of which do not display the high rates of repetitive firing that are characteristics of cerebellar Purkinje neurons.
source: Interestingly, INaR has now been identified in over 20 types of neurons, many of which do not display the high rates of repetitive firing that are characteristics of cerebellar Purkinje neurons, suggesting that the role(s) of INaR in the regulation of membrane excitability are diverse, and likely distinct, in different neuronal cell types (Lewis and Raman, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lewis and Raman, 2014.

claim: The role(s) of INaR in the regulation of membrane excitability are diverse, and likely distinct, in different neuronal cell types.
source: Interestingly, INaR has now been identified in over 20 types of neurons, many of which do not display the high rates of repetitive firing that are characteristics of cerebellar Purkinje neurons, suggesting that the role(s) of INaR in the regulation of membrane excitability are diverse, and likely distinct, in different neuronal cell types (Lewis and Raman, 2014).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that INaR is found in diverse neuron types.

claim: The accumulation of Nav channels in a slow-inactivated state functions as a homeostatic brake on repetitive firing in serotonergic raphe neurons.
source: Recent studies conducted on serotonergic raphe neurons, for example, suggest that the accumulation of Nav channels in a slow-inactivated state functions as a homeostatic brake on repetitive firing (Navarro et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Navarro et al., 2020.

claim: INaR has been implicated in several inherited and acquired neurological diseases including paroxysmal extreme pain disorder, paramyotonia congenita, chemotherapy-induced neuropathy, and epilepsy.
source: In addition, INaR has been implicated in several inherited and acquired neurological diseases (Lewis and Raman, 2014), including paroxysmal extreme pain disorder, paramyotonia congenita (Jarecki et al., 2010), and chemotherapy-induced neuropathy (Lewis and Raman, 2014; Sittl et al., 2012), as well as epilepsy (Hargus et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Postnatal day 12–16 (P12–P16) male and female C57BL6/J mice were used in the experiments.
source: Postnatal day 12–16 (P12–P16) male and female C57BL6/J (Jackson laboratories) mice were used in the experiments reported here.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.
